# Orientation

This project uses Tiller to run its SDLC workflow. Specs, decomposition,
planning, and acceptance gates live in `.tiller/`, under git, beside the code
they describe. This file is your front door: it explains what Tiller is, the
rules you must follow, how to work, and where things live. It depends on nothing
but a filesystem, a shell, and the `tiller` CLI.

## What Tiller is

Tiller holds the structure, the gates, and the state. You, the agent, do the
reasoning. The human approves at the gates. And Tiller guides rather than
controls: it offers structure and guidance you should follow, surfaced honestly
as guidance, not walls. The one boundary that genuinely holds sits outside
Tiller, at the merge, which only the human performs. Everything you do
ultimately attributes to the person who directed you.

## The rules you must follow

- Drive work to the edge of done and stop. You may propose, build, attach
  evidence through gates, run gates, and open PRs. A gate is the human's
  decision, not the human's keyboard: on an explicit instruction naming the
  nodes you may run `approve` yourself, stating exactly what you are about to
  record and reporting what you recorded. A declarative past-tense claim
  ("they're all approved") is authorization to record only when the set is
  unambiguous: verify the recorded state first, then record, then report the
  delta. `attest`, `sync --accept-fast-forward`, and the merge to
  done are never yours to run, even on instruction; hand the human the exact
  command.
- Mutate state only through `tiller`. The state files are machine-owned: never
  hand-edit `epic.yml`, `feature.yml`, `task.yml`, the event stream,
  or `board.md`, and never hand-edit this file. Every change to state
  lands through a command, so the event stream and the gate records stay honest.
  The one `.yml` you own is the manifest, `.tiller/tiller.yml`: its
  configuration (gates, owners, inputs) is human-owned, so edit freely.
- End every piece of reasoning by recording it through a command. The reasoning
  is yours; the recording is the CLI's. A conclusion that is not written down
  through `tiller` did not happen.
- Commit the state Tiller writes. Every command records into git-tracked files
  under `.tiller/`, and Tiller never commits them for you. The commit is part
  of the work: commit the state delta with, or right after, the change it
  describes, using plain `git` and this project's own commit conventions.
  One requirement rides on top of those conventions rather than replacing them:
  a commit you author while executing a task carries the task's id somewhere in its message,
  so `git log` can walk from any commit to the node that explains it. An
  uncommitted `.tiller/` change is not shared state and is not a review
  surface. The merge is still the human's; committing is not. A diff that touches
  only `.tiller/` never needs a pull request: planning state, gate records,
  and events are CLI-written audit records, so commit them directly, a mid-task
  delta on the feature branch it belongs to and everything else straight on the
  integration branch. The PR ceremony is for code.
- Follow the recovery protocol when a command refuses. Exit `1` is a business
  answer to reason about, usually a red gate or an illegal transition: fix the
  work and try again, do not escalate. Exit `2` or `3` is a bad call or a
  broken environment: fix the call. When you are unsure what is legal from here,
  `tiller status <noun> <node>` names the legal next moves with nothing executed.
  That one-node oracle is also the surface that reports `active_basis` drift,
  a spec or contract edited out from under approved work; the bare
  `tiller status` project summary does not, so ask the node when a gate
  refuses on a basis you did not expect to have moved.
- Name a node to the human by its key path with the id in parentheses, for
  example `form-engine/nrca-form-loading (F-79dh3q)`. A task's key path
  carries all three segments and reads
  `form-engine/nrca-form-loading/schema-transcription (T-k3p9w6)`.
  A question is never keyed: name it by its id and short title. Use the full
  statement when the question itself is the subject.
  The rule covers every surface you author, readout notes, hand-offs,
  summaries, and lists alike: an epic, feature, or task id never appears
  without its key path, because a bare id sends the developer off to look up
  what it points at. Bare ids belong inside commands, where they are always
  valid. A commit subject reads the same way: the bare task id satisfies
  traceability there. A pull request title carries the reviewed node's full key
  path with its id. Its body names the work riding that review, the task's
  parent feature at task grain, or the tasks and features at a coarser grain.
- Work inside this repository. Tiller's guidance is complete in the project:
  this file, the skills `tiller guide` serves, and the command output.
  Never go hunting outside the project directory for Tiller documentation or
  schema shapes. Leave the project only where the developer points you.
- Report through the readout. At a seam, `tiller readout <seam>` prints a
  block; at a human gate the command prints one itself; either way,
  reproduce it verbatim as the last thing in your reply, with your own
  account under `Notes from this run` ahead of it. The block closes the
  reply, nothing follows it, so its `**Next:**` line is the final line
  the developer reads. It renders the same whoever is driving, so the
  developer reads one format rather than yours.

## How to work

Run `tiller status` to see where things stand, then `tiller guide` to load the
skill for the moment. With no argument, `tiller guide` names the skill that fits
the current state; with a skill name it prints that skill in full. When you are
choosing the next seam, name the route to the developer and stop for their go;
work already moving inside a seam keeps moving. The pause is the developer's
moment to correct your picture of the project and to add the context the
design docs do not carry; conventions worth keeping belong in `AGENTS.md`.

Onboarding starts at the scaffold, and it is three commands, not two. A bare
repo becomes a Tiller project with
`tiller init --key <key> --kind <archetype> --name "<project name>"` (add
`--design <dir>` to import a design folder in the same move). Registering a
person and selecting your identity are two separate, deliberate acts, so the
next two commands are not one: a human runs
`tiller owner add <you> --name "<full name>"` to put you on the roster,
and an agent runs it only on an explicit human instruction naming both the id
and the name, and only then
does `tiller join --as <you>` select that registered id as who is working
this checkout. join can register no one: an id absent from the roster,
whichever of `--as`, `TILLER_OWNER`, or the checkout's own
`.tiller/identity.yml` supplied it, is refused rather than added. The
roster is not add-only: `tiller owner remove <id>` retires someone later, the
same human-gated act, refusing while they still hold live work. Do not
skip either step: without them there is no owner here, so the first
`tiller add` exits `3`, `check readiness` reports the empty roster as a gap,
and step 2 of the route below can never match, since it is scoped to the
owner. Then `tiller check readiness` confirms the inputs and manifest are
in order. The first seam is `decompose`, turning those inputs into a draft
tree for the human to approve: name it and stop for the developer's go.
From there the route below carries the work forward.

Every feature is born unclaimed, in the pool, whoever ran `add` or
approved the amendment that minted it included; claiming one is a separate,
later act. Before you `start` a feature, or `start`, `submit`, or `resume` a
task, claim that feature: `tiller claim feature <key>` takes an unclaimed one outright, or,
on one someone else already holds, refuses naming them, and you retry with
`--from <id>` restating that holder, only on an explicit human instruction
naming the handoff. `tiller release feature <key>` returns a claim to the
pool. `tiller reassign feature <key> --to <owner> --reason <text>` is the
human's own handoff, never yours to run even on instruction. The judgment
verbs, `approve`, `attest`, `answer`, `eval`, and `check`, bind to no claim:
reviewing, verifying, and answering are exactly the acts a non-claimant
performs.

Review does not have to land once per task. `review_grain` records where
it lands instead: `task` by default, `feature`, or `epic`. It lives in the
project's `tiller.yml`, an epic's `epic.yml`, and a feature's `feature.yml`,
absence inheriting downward and the most specific explicit setting winning.
A feature cannot itself say `epic`, since riding its epic's PR is inheritance,
not an override. Set it only on an explicit human instruction naming the node
and grain, through `tiller configure project`, `configure epic <key>`,
`configure feature <key>`, or the matching `approve --review-grain` gate.
State what you will record and report what you recorded.

Invalid stored grain values refuse the tree rather than defaulting. If
`configure project` refuses an unsupported scalar or flow-mapping
`execution` shape, rewrite that human-owned manifest setting as block-form
YAML and rerun the command; never edit machine-owned node state.

Finish and sync submitted work before changing a review grain that would affect it.
An affected feature review or a task in `in_progress`, `check`, or
`in_review` locks the change. Entering or leaving epic grain also locks once
an affected feature records its branch. Never hand-edit state around a refusal.
Every live feature riding one epic review branch must have the same feature claimant.
The epic's owner remains attribution. An overridden feature finishes its own
review and reaches `done` before the epic review opens.
Coarse submit still enforces active basis, questions, reviewed assumptions, claims, and retired ancestors.
Even after gates are green, those refusals remain.

The route is read off recorded state, in this order, first match wins. It is
the same walk `tiller guide` runs with no argument, so the two never disagree.

1. No epics recorded: the seam is `decompose`.
2. A task you hold in `ready` or `in_progress` with no operative
   open question against it or an ancestor: the seam is `execute`.
   The alternative arm in this same step is a coarse review at its finish
   line. It becomes reachable when the last live task enters
   `in_review`, meaning every live task under the reviewed feature is
   `in_review` or `done`. At epic grain that condition holds across
   every feature riding the epic branch, and every independent override is
   already `done`.
   A task in hand outranks the frontier.
   Both execution alternatives in this step are scoped to you: the task arm
   by its recorded owner, and the coarse finish line by the feature claimant
   or the epic review's derived live owner.
   In both cases, never tell the developer the frontier shows only their own work.
   Every remaining route step answers for the project.
   A task under an unclaimed feature carries no owner, so it matches nobody
   until someone runs `tiller claim feature <key>`; pool work is nobody's
   next move before then.
   Under a coarse review grain, finishing one task routes straight to the
   next ready task on the same review branch. Feature grain ends with
   `tiller eval feature`, `tiller check feature`, then
   `tiller submit feature`. Epic grain repeats the loop across features
   with one common claimant and ends in `tiller submit epic`.
   A coarse submit refusal still names the active basis, question, assumption
   review, claim, or retired ancestor to clear.
3. A `proposed` amendment awaiting approval: a human wait, not a seam.
   Name `tiller approve amendment` as the developer's move and stop.
   It outranks the plan gate below and the frontier under it, because
   approving a staged reshape can supersede or cancel the very feature that
   gate would have approved. Several amendments can be open at once, and the
   route names the first by id.
4. A feature in `specced` awaiting its plan gate: a human wait, not a
   seam. Name `tiller approve feature` as the developer's move and stop.
   It outranks the frontier: finishing the gate you opened comes before
   opening a new spec.
5. The frontier: a live feature still in `draft`,
   whose recorded `depends_on` targets are all settled (done, or
   cancelled), and whose own epic's recorded dependencies are settled the
   same way; an epic-grain edge gates the epic's features exactly as a
   feature-grain edge gates the feature.
   The seam is `specify`, and the feature is the project's,
   not any one owner's. A draft still waiting on unfinished work is skipped,
   not suggested. Among the eligible, the recorded soft order chooses first,
   the owning epic's place in it and then the feature's own, with flow
   position only breaking what the lists leave open.
   The lifecycle is the queue: `draft` is the backlog,
   `specced` and `ready` are on deck, `active` is in progress, and
   only the human's go pulls a feature forward. Specifying one feature when its
   turn comes, rather than every feature up front, is what keeps a large tree
   tractable. Ordering lives in `depends_on` and lanes are owners. A
   recorded soft order refines that: where the graph leaves peers unordered,
   the stated sequence arranges the render and the route's suggestion, and it
   never gates; working in another order stays legal. Two disjoint dependency
   chains on the frontier are two owners working in parallel, not a layer of
   planning between the tree and the work.
6. A task in `in_review`: a human wait rather than a seam. Surface it and
   stop. The exception is a task whose PR review requested changes, which
   re-enters `execute` through `tiller resume task <id> --reason "..."`.
   Under a coarse review grain the task itself carries no PR; the reviewed
   feature or epic does. A task in `in_review` whose feature or epic has
   not yet recorded its own PR or review ref is not a human wait at all:
   item 2 above already names the actual next step, gates or submit, and the
   walk moves on rather than stopping here. Once that reviewed node's PR is
   recorded, the wait names it instead of the task: the feature PR is open,
   awaiting your merge, or, one level up, the epic PR is open, awaiting your
   merge.
7. Drafts exist but every one waits on unfinished dependencies: a blocked
   frontier is a named wait, not an empty tree. Surface what it waits on and
   stop. Otherwise this is the true caught-up terminal. When Unclaimed is
   non-empty, keep its full count and the concrete
   `tiller claim feature <key>` command for its first dependency-ranked feature
   exactly as guide and the readout render them. The notice makes no ownership
   claim; the feature remains in the pool until the claim succeeds. Only an
   empty pool is the plain nothing-due answer.

A route can select a later legal task while carrying one advisory for the first
earlier owned task held by operative direct or inherited open questions. Keep
the selected target first. Its `Order note` names that skipped task, the first
question by short title and Q-id, and
`tiller answer question <Q-id> --answer "..."`, with any remaining blocker
count. Answering one question may leave others. The note is not a replacement
route: `**Next:**` remains the selected signpost and does not repeat it.

`tiller guide` serves seven skills:

- `orient`: you need the next move. Read state, name the route above to the
  developer, and stop.
- `decompose`: inputs exist but the tree does not. Lay a draft epic and feature
  tree for the human to approve.
- `specify`: a feature is in draft. Write its specification, its acceptance
  contract, and its tasks in one pass, then `tiller spec feature`.
- `execute`: you hold a ready or in-progress task, or a coarse review
  is at its finish line. Run the work loop to the resolved review surface, then stop.
- `mend-drift`: `tiller drift` reports a candidate. Read it, draft
  the smallest honest fix, and stop for the human to approve.
- `amend`: a change reshapes the plan rather than extends it. Sort the
  corrections from the casualties, stage the reshape as one amendment, and stop
  for the human's `approve amendment`.
- `intake`: the developer hands you a document written outside the tree
  that makes a case for change, or `tiller intake` already landed one and
  opened an amendment with nothing staged. Read it whole, stage the mapping as
  one sourced amendment, and stop for the human's `approve amendment`.

`tiller drift` is a check the route above does not run on its own: run it
yourself, and when it reports a candidate, the seam is `mend-drift`. One more
seam sits outside that walk for a reason of its own: no field in the tree
says a reshape is due. When the change in front of you reshapes the plan rather
than extends it, because the developer says so or one upstream change cascades
across a dozen nodes, the seam is `amend`. Name what you think it is and let the
developer confirm before anything is staged: staging records proposals and
executes nothing, and the human's `approve amendment` is the one act that
applies the batch. Intake sits outside the walk too, for a different reason:
it is operator-initiated on feedback arriving, not a seam the route computes
from recorded state, so land the document and stage the mapping the moment
the developer hands it to you, or `tiller intake` already has.

Process is Tiller's; craft is the repo's own. How you write the code, the testing
discipline, and the architecture live in this project's `AGENTS.md` and
`CLAUDE.md`, not in a Tiller skill. The skills are opinionated about the shape
and gating of the work and silent on the content of the implementation.

## Where things live

Everything Tiller owns is under `.tiller/` at the repo root:

- `tiller.yml` is the manifest: the project archetype, the owners, the inputs,
  and the gates.
- `design/` holds the durable design docs the tree is decomposed from.
- `epics/<epic-key>/` holds each epic, its `features/<feature-key>/` folders,
  and within a feature its `feature.md` spec, `feature.eval.md` acceptance
  contract, `feature.yml` state, and `tasks/<task-key>/` folders, each
  holding a `task.md` implementation spec beside its `task.yml` state.
- `plans/`, `decisions/`, and `events/` hold execution plans, decision records
  and open questions, and the append-only event stream.

For anything live, who holds what and what is where, read `tiller status` rather
than this file.
